question_text: Express the complex number −√3 + i in the modulus-amplitude form.

mark_split.label: Find the amplitude θ from the quadrant and write r(cos θ + i sin θ)

recall_prompt: Say how you would write a complex number in modulus-amplitude form — what two numbers you need and how the quadrant fixes the angle.
insider_note: A calculator gives θ = −π/6, which is the fourth-quadrant point (√3, −1), not this number. (−√3, 1) is in the second quadrant, so θ = π − π/6 = 5π/6 — the quadrant sentence is what earns the second mark.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Find r
steps.margin_note: First mark. x = −√3, y = 1, so r = √(3 + 1) = 2.

recall.must_convey: That x = −√3, y = 1 and the modulus r = √(3 + 1) = 2.
accept: x is minus root three, y is one, r is root of three plus one which is two
the modulus is root four equals two
r equals root x squared plus y squared, that is two
three plus one is four, root of that is two

steps.why: (−√3)² = 3 — the sign disappears under the square. r = 2 goes in front of the bracket; the negative x is used only to place the point in the second quadrant.
common_mistakes: Reading the number as −3 + i and getting r = √10.

steps.label: Find θ and write the form
steps.margin_note: Second mark. tan θ = −1/√3. The point (−√3, 1) is in the second quadrant, so θ = π − π/6 = 5π/6. Check: 2 cos(5π/6) = −√3 and 2 sin(5π/6) = 1.

recall.must_convey: That tan θ = −1/√3 with the point in the second quadrant gives θ = 5π/6, so the form is 2(cos 5π/6 + i sin 5π/6).
accept: tan theta is minus one by root three and the point is in the second quadrant so theta is five pi by six
the form is two times cos five pi by six plus i sin five pi by six
second quadrant, theta equals pi minus pi by six equals five pi by six
point second quadrant lo undi kabatti theta five pi by six
amplitude five pi by six and modulus two

steps.why: tan θ = −1/√3 is true for −π/6 and for 5π/6. A negative x with positive y is the second quadrant, so the amplitude is π − (acute angle) = 5π/6. The quadrant line, not the tan value, is what fixes the answer.
common_mistakes: Taking θ = −π/6 from the calculator — that is the fourth-quadrant point (√3, −1).
Taking θ = π/6, the first-quadrant point (√3, 1).
